detail: supported
Compute the distance: $dist = \|\vec{dir}\|$ [S1, unofficial].

The notes explicitly state 'Compute direction and distance: dir = (p2 - p1); dist = dir.length();'. The claim states 'Compute the distance: $dist = ||dir||$'. In vector mathematics, the notation $||dir||$ represents the magnitude (or length) of the vector `dir`. Therefore, the claim accurately reflects the operation described in the evidence.
supported

A global visibility function $\hat{V}(\omega)$ representing the average visibility from points on the surfaces inside a voxel through the entire scene along direction $\omega$, used to model spatial correlation between voxels [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that a global visibility function V_hat(omega) represents the average visibility from points on the surfaces inside a voxel through the entire scene along direction omega, and is used to model spatial correlation between voxels. Source [S2] explicitly defines V_hat(omega) as 'the average visibility from points on the surfaces A inside a voxel through the entire scene along omega' (Equation 25 and surrounding text). Furthermore, the text explains that 'modeling the global visibility naturally captures spatial correlation' and that the method 'explicitly tracking the global AIV V_hat_i ... naturally incorporates correlation'. Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
Traditional volumetric models assume transmittance is exponential and cannot model spatial correlation, producing incorrect results even if per-voxel visibilities are identical [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that traditional volumetric models assume transmittance is exponential, cannot model spatial correlation, and produce incorrect results even if per-voxel visibilities are identical. Source [S2] explicitly confirms all these points: it states that 'Existing works show that when spatial correlation exists, transmittance is no longer exponential,' that traditional models 'fail to recognize the correlation,' and that they 'produce an incorrect result by applying the Beer-Lambert law' even when configurations have 'identical per-voxel visibilities.'

It accumulates voxel contributions using the product of their individual AIV values to correctly handle positive and negative correlations between voxels, which traditional Beer-Lambert law fails to do [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the method accumulates voxel contributions using the product of their individual AIV values to handle positive and negative correlations, which traditional Beer-Lambert law fails to do. Source [S2] explicitly defines AIV (aggregated interior visibility) as the average visibility from points on surfaces inside a voxel. It illustrates that traditional volumetric models (Beer-Lambert law) fail to recognize correlation and produce incorrect results when voxels are positively or negatively correlated, even if per-voxel visibilities are identical. The source further explains that by explicitly tracking global AIV, the method naturally incorporates correlation and produces correct accumulation results, implying the use of AIV in the accumulation process to achieve this. The notes provided also directly quote the claim's phrasing. Therefore, the evidence supports the claim.
supported
